newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries narrowly higher at midday.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries narrowly higher at midday.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were slightly higher at midday on Tuesday, trading near the bottom of the session's ranges.

Trading was choppy during the first half of the session, traders said. Prices opened firm and traded in the plus column through midday. The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up as much as 9/32 in mid-morning activity. By noon EDT/1600 GMT, however, it was up just 2/32, yielding 6.82 percent.
"Trading was in a very narrow range," said Larry Dyer, bond market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
Dyer said the economic data that the market got during the morning was not a significant influence.

"The data were near expectations and it wasn't important data to begin with in terms of the market's outlook," he said. "There's a little more data due this afternoon which you can characterize the same way."

In one Tuesday morning report, the seasonally-adjusted BTM/Schroders weekly chain store sales index rose 0.7 percent in the latest week after falling 0.5 percent a week earlier. Also, the Richmond Federal Reserve Bank said its manufacturing shipments index rose to 21 from 15 in April.
The Richmond Fed's manufacturing new orders index fell to 16 from 25 in April and the service revenues index fell to 26 in May from 33 in April.

The last economic item of the trading session will be the Lynch, Jones & Ryan Redbook weekly chain store sales report. Officially released at 1455 EDT/1855 GMT but typically known in the market before then, that index rose 0.5 percent in the most recently reported week. A forecast for the week ended June 7 was not available.
"We're all just waiting for (the government's report on Thursday on May) retail sales," said Dyer.

The May retail sales data due on Thursday and the May Producer Price Index (PPI) due on Friday are expected to be friendly toward the bond market which benefits from news of a slower economy and subdued inflation.
Retail sales are expected to be up just modestly after declining in April. The PPI is forcast to be up 0.1 percent.

Traders said some dealer and hedge fund selling brought the market down from its highs toward midday. Also, awareness that Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan is scheduled to deliver a speech in New York this evening could be injecting an element of caution, they said.
Dyer said there was some arbitrage selling of 10-year maturities and buying of five- and 30-year securities.

"That spread got fairly wide," Dyer said, explaining that the Treasury's announcement on Monday that it would cancel two of its six 10-year Treasury note auctions for the year made the 10-year sector of the maturity curve relatively rich.
Some central bank buying of U.S. securities was rumored.

Analysts said the spread between the two-year note and the Federal funds rate would have a hard time narrowing further unless Thursday's retail sales report was even more friendly for the market than has been forecast.
The spread between the two-year note yield and the Fed funds rate stood at 63 basis points at midday.

"I'm getting a nosebleed here," said Dyer. "You're not hearing talk about a Fed ease which is what it takes to get two-years flat to Fed funds. I would think we've priced in a good deal of any slowdown we'd see in the economic data."
At midday, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was priced at 97-17/32, up 2/32 from Monday's close and yielding 6.82 percent.

Three-month bill rates were down four basis points to 4.88 percent. Six-month bill rates were up one basis point to 5.19 percent and year bill rates were down one basis point to 5.41 percent. Two-year notes were up 1/32 to 100-7/32, yielding 6.13 percent. Five-year notes were priced at 100-10/32 to yield 6.43 percent. Ten-year notes were trading at 100-20/32, up 1/32, to yield 6.54 percent.
(( -- North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1679))
